contributions: Rubrics synthesized per question from the raw waveform rather than from a transcript, so every criterion is anchored to acoustic evidence actually present in the clip

Rubric evolution conditioned on the sampled rollout group: new criteria are elicited from where stronger and weaker rollouts diverge, including negatively-phrased ones that capture recurring failure modes a positive criterion cannot express
A variance filter that prunes any rubric whose verdicts are identical across all rollouts, on the explicit ground that such a criterion contributes nothing to the group-relative advantage
A linear length penalty introduced to counterbalance the rubric reward, which otherwise pays for longer traces that satisfy more criteria
A measurement of the evolution itself: the share of newly generated rubrics in the active set over training
limitations: The paper has no limitations section. What a reader should weigh: the headline is a rubric method whose ablation attributes most of the movement to ordinary RL — 10.00 of 12.80 points on MMAU — with the entire rubric apparatus, static plus evolving plus length penalty, worth 2.80. The method also hinges on a strong proprietary generator and judge, and the paper shows it falling below plain GRPO when that is weakened, which makes the result conditional on a component the authors do not control and cannot release. Nothing accounts for the cost of that dependency: a judge call is issued per rubric per rollout per group per step, and no compute or wall-clock comparison against the GRPO baseline appears. Both reward weights are selected by sweeps on the same benchmarks the headline table reports. There is one policy backbone, one training corpus, greedy decoding only, and no seeds or variance anywhere. Finally, the claim that the rubrics make reasoning grounded in the audio is supported by accuracy on a perception split rather than by any direct check that the traces cite acoustic evidence — the mechanism is plausible and the measurement is still downstream accuracy.
method: For each question an audio-capable model is fed the raw waveform, the query and the gold answer and returns one binary, positively-phrased criterion per dimension of a fixed taxonomy, with importance weights summing to one. At every RL step, conditioned on the group of sampled rollouts and the rubric set retained from the previous iteration, that same model proposes up to N new non-redundant criteria, judges every rubric against every rollout as a binary verdict, and has negative-polarity judgements flipped so a 1 always denotes a good outcome. Each rubric's within-group standard deviation is then computed and any rubric with zero variance is pruned — satisfied by all rollouts or by none, it assigns every rollout the same verdict and cannot contribute advantage — with the top M most discriminative survivors kept and re-weighted. The rubric score is the weighted sum of a rollout's verdicts. The total per-rollout reward adds the outcome reward (accuracy plus a format term), the rubric reward scaled by gamma, and an overthinking penalty linear in trace length scaled by delta; accuracy-only RLVR is recovered at gamma = delta = 0, and the whole thing is optimized with GRPO. The policy is Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with 8 rollouts per example, trained on 40,176 audio-text pairs derived from AVQA on 4 H100 GPUs, with Gemini-3.1-Pro serving as both rubric generator and judge, evaluated greedily on MMAU Test-mini, MMAR and MMSU.
one_liner: Supervises audio reasoning with per-question rubrics generated from the raw waveform, and keeps the signal alive as the policy improves by regenerating the rubrics from the model's own rollouts each step and pruning any criterion that every rollout satisfies or none does.
problem: Reward designs for audio reasoning are complementary in their weaknesses. An outcome reward supervises only the final answer, so a model can reach it without attending to the audio at all. Process rewards score the reasoning but rely on coarse hand-written criteria that check the surface quality of a trace rather than whether it is grounded in the acoustic evidence, so a fluent well-structured passage unsupported by the clip is rewarded. A single fixed rubric also mismatches the heterogeneity of the task — some questions turn on perception alone and soliciting extra reasoning for them adds cost and hallucination risk, others need multi-step inference — and any static criterion decays as the policy improves, because once a model reliably satisfies it the criterion stops discriminating and its gradient vanishes.

relevance.reasoning-evaluation: Its transferable contribution is a criterion for when an evaluation signal is worth computing at all: a rubric whose verdict is identical across every rollout in a group is discarded, because under group-relative advantage it can move nothing. That is the same quantity this archive has just met from another direction, where a prompt whose eight rollouts are all wrong produces zero advantage and contributes no gradient. Two unrelated papers, one on audio rubrics and one on experience distillation, independently identify within-group variation rather than signal strength as what decides whether supervision is usable — which suggests reporting it should be routine rather than incidental. The paper also demonstrates the failure mode of an evaluation signal that is optimized directly: past a rubric weight of 0.5 accuracy declines because the policy optimizes for satisfying criteria rather than for being right, and a length penalty had to be added because more criteria are satisfied by longer traces. Any rubric-scored evaluation in this archive should expect both.

results: Against its own base policy the method gains 12.80 points on MMAU (65.20 to 78.00) and 6.58 on MMSU (59.28 to 65.86), and it leads every similar-size open model on all three benchmarks, reaching 65.80 overall on MMAR against 65.30 for the strongest training-based baseline. It edges the proprietary frontier on one benchmark (78.00 against Gemini-3.1-Pro's 77.60 on MMAU) and remains far below it on the others (65.86 against 82.60 on MMSU, 65.80 against 77.50 on MMAR). The ablation is the most informative table and it cuts against the framing: of the 12.80-point MMAU gain, reinforcement learning alone accounts for 10.00 (65.20 to 75.20), static rubrics add 1.00, making them evolve adds a further 1.00, and the length penalty adds 0.80. Each component is real and none is large. Both weights show interior optima rather than monotone benefit — the rubric weight peaks at 0.5 and declines beyond it, which the paper reads as an overly large rubric term downweighting the accuracy reward so the policy optimizes for satisfying criteria rather than answering correctly, and the length penalty peaks at 0.15 with a larger value compressing the trace enough to weaken reasoning. The evolution measurement supports the mechanism: newly generated rubrics grow from roughly 35% of the adopted set early in training to about 60% by the end, so the variance filter is steadily retiring criteria the policy has mastered. The sharpest dependency is on the generator and judge — replacing Gemini-3.1-Pro with a weaker audio model drops performance on all three benchmarks, in the paper's own words even below the vanilla GRPO baseline, with the training curves separating after a brief warmup.
